# **1\. Problem Description**

The problem that we are attempting to solve is to ~~aid college~~ help pickleball ~~captains in selecting a team consisting of two male~~ players ~~and two female players~~ find doubles partners whose court coverage and skills complement ~~each other across several different doubles pairings. The scope of the problem we are trying to solve~~ their own. One motivating use case is ~~the~~ Major League Pickleball–style tournaments, where a team of two men and two women competes in women’s doubles, men’s doubles, and two games of mixed doubles. ~~Due to the nature of this format, DUPR describes the teamwork aspect as follows: “teamwork is as critical as speed or technique on the court and is a big part of the sport's community aspect.” Determining the optimal team combinations requires~~ This format illustrates why partner compatibility matters across different pairings \[1\]. Finding complementary partners can require a large time commitment, as players need to practice and play with a wide range of partners. ~~Then it is up to the discretion of a small group of~~ Players and team captains ~~and coaches to make countless decisions based~~ often rely on ~~empirical logic.~~ observations from these sessions when choosing partners. This challenge is personally relevant to our team, as a member of our team competes in collegiate pickleball tournaments for Purdue and frequently plays with a wide range of partners as rosters and availability change. Our MVP focuses on recommending doubles partners to players. Complete four-player lineup optimization is a possible future extension, not a requirement for using the matching engine.

This problem is not limited to the Purdue pickleball team; it extends across one of the fastest-growing sports as a whole. According to the Sports & Fitness Industry Association, pickleball participation in the United States grew ~~by 479%~~ from 4.2 million participants in 2020 to 24.3 million in 2025, ~~and pickleball became one~~ an increase of ~~the top 25 most-played sports and activities in the United States.~~ approximately 479% \[7\]. The rapid growth of the sport ~~shows both~~ suggests a ~~need~~ growing potential user base; player research is still needed to establish demand for partner ~~matching~~ matching. Existing tools provide ratings, performance analysis, and ~~an opportunity for those who solve this problem. The existing tools on the market~~ some coordination metrics; our proposed focus ~~on~~ is using individual ~~performance but fail~~ drill measurements to ~~evaluate how individual playing styles will work as a team.~~ recommend complementary partners. For instance, DUPR, the standard for pickleball ratings, calculates team strength by averaging the partners’ ratings but ~~provides no insight into relevant teamwork metrics.~~ an aggregate rating does not directly describe direction-specific court coverage \[2\]. Another popular pickleball analysis tool, PB Vision, provides more detailed insight into players’ skill ratings ~~but is unable to judge~~ and includes partner coordination in its Kitchen Game assessment \[4\]. We will evaluate the ~~compatibility~~ added value of ~~doubles partners.~~ our drill-based matching approach rather than assume existing tools lack all teamwork analysis. The main question we are trying to answer is: ~~What is the best combination of four players to provide~~ Which doubles partners have complementary court ~~coverage,~~ coverage and ~~how should they be paired?~~ shot strengths, and does this information improve recommendations beyond skill level alone? Our project would utilize camera-driven measurements.

## **Customer evidence and validation**

The team member experience described above is our initial internal stakeholder evidence. We will supplement it with interviews with approximately 5–8 collegiate and recreational players about how they currently find partners, difficulties they encounter, and which explanations would help them trust a recommendation. We will document examples and quotations with permission and connect the findings to requirements. Coaches or captains may provide additional domain advice, but direct player feedback will guide the main workflow. These interviews are planned; we are not presenting them as completed customer research.

# **2\. Solution Description**

Our proposed solution is a ~~camera enabled Iphone~~ camera-enabled iPhone application designed to help collegiate pickleball players and teams make data-driven decisions. Players will complete a set of standardized ~~drills,~~ individual drills and record their actions through the mobile application. Then, the system will analyze these recordings to create player profiles describing movement, court coverage, and shot strengths. These results will also be augmented by manually inputted data like handedness and preferred play style. These profiles will then be compared against other ~~eligible~~ registered players ~~on~~ who have completed the ~~team’s roster~~ required assessments and meet the user’s matching filters to generate ranked partner recommendations based on complementary strengths, predicted coverage gaps, and additional factors such as location, skill level, preferred court side, and play style. The system will also provide visual explanations of each recommendation so players, captains, and coaches can understand why a particular pairing may be effective. Players can receive recommendations without belonging to a managed team or obtaining coach approval. The interface will center on drill recording, assessment results, player profiles, and partner recommendations.

The system will use a client-server architecture consisting of a React Native mobile application, a FastAPI backend, background video-analysis workers, a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database, and private video storage in Amazon S3. Through the mobile application, players will select a drill, receive camera placement and calibration guidance, and complete live setup checks before recording. Once a drill is recorded, the video will be uploaded to private storage and submitted to a background analysis pipeline using Celery workers and a Redis job queue. The analysis pipeline will use computer-vision techniques to calibrate the court, track player movement, identify ball events, and score individual drill attempts. The resulting measurements, confidence values, sample counts, and coverage information will be stored in the player's profile. The backend will then use a comparison algorithm on eligible player profiles and return ranked partner recommendations, individual and combined court-coverage visualizations, and explanations of the factors that contributed to each suggested pairing.

The technical complexity of our solution comes from integrating mobile video capture, computer vision, asynchronous processing, spatial data, persistent player profiles, and partner-ranking logic into a single system. The project must reliably transform ordinary smartphone video into meaningful pickleball measurements by validating camera setup, calibrating the court, tracking players and the ball, identifying valid drill attempts, and handling uncertain or incomplete observations. These measurements must then be converted into interpretable court-coverage and shot-strength profiles that can be compared under consistent drill conditions. There is also no obvious formula for determining whether two players are complementary partners, so the team must design and evaluate a configurable matching model that considers coverage gaps, complementary strengths, skill level, play style, and other relevant factors. The proposed innovation is using video-derived movement and shot measurements not only for individual performance analysis, but to support explainable, pair-specific partner recommendations for players seeking compatible partners, including collegiate ~~team selection.~~ players. The intended value ~~that this would provide would~~ is to make ~~team~~ potential partner compatibility ~~measurable and explainable, while reducing the effort~~ easier to compare ~~potential lineups.~~ and explain; its usefulness will be evaluated with players.

## **Drills and player measurements**

We will pilot predictable lateral feeds, unpredictable lateral feeds, and forehand/backhand target returns. These are candidate drills, with final choices informed by experienced players and optional coaching advice. A starting pilot protocol is approximately 20 valid feeds per drill, balanced across the tested directions, repeated on two separate sessions. This is a proposed starting point, not a claim that the sample size is sufficient. Human feeders and ball machines will use defined starting positions, target areas, and timing ranges; feed type and drill conditions will be recorded.

| Measurement | What we will measure | How it supports matching |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Directional movement | Player displacement and travel time in court coordinates, grouped by direction. | Identify movement differences under comparable drill conditions. |
| Response-time proxy | Time from a visible feed event to the first detected movement. | Compare prescribed and reactive stages separately; this is not a clinical reaction-time measurement. |
| Return success | Successful returns divided by confidently scored valid feeds, grouped by direction or shot type. | Distinguish reaching a ball from successfully returning it. |
| Court coverage | Estimated return success for tested court regions and time windows from defined starting positions. | Highlight complementary strengths and areas where both partners have limited coverage. |

A successful attempt requires the player to return the ball over the net with its first landing in the drill’s defined opposing-court area. Confidently observed misses, net failures, and out-of-bounds returns count as failures. Invalid feeds and uncertain outcomes are excluded from both the success count and the number of scored attempts, with exclusion reasons shown. Unsupported regions remain unknown rather than being treated as failures.

We will use repeated sessions to check measurement stability and report valid sample counts, exclusions, and uncertainty, including 95% Wilson intervals for return proportions \[13\]. We will choose minimum sample and precision criteria after the pilot and before the final evaluation. If a category is too noisy, we will collect more comparable attempts, simplify the category, or mark it insufficient for matching. Session-level variation will be reported because repeated feeds are not independent players.

## **Initial partner matching approach**

The engine will first identify registered candidates with sufficient comparable drill data and apply user-selected filters such as location and skill range. It will then compare complementary coverage, skill compatibility, and court-side preferences. Self-reported play style will initially be displayed as context; we will only assign it a numerical contribution if stakeholder research and evaluation support a clear definition.

A candidate scoring form is: pair score \= wC × C \+ wS × S \+ wP × P, where the nonnegative weights sum to 1\. C represents combined coverage under shared tested scenarios; S represents compatibility with the user’s desired skill range; and P represents agreement with supported court-side preferences. The initial coverage proxy will average the higher of the two players’ measured return-success values across comparable region/time scenarios. This is a simple assignment-based estimate, not a measured joint success probability; communication and collisions require paired evaluation. Only tested starting positions will be compared.

For example, if a player covers left-side scenarios well but struggles on the right, a candidate with stronger right-side coverage may rank above a similarly rated candidate with the same left-side strength. Weights and skill-range scaling will be selected using pilot data and fixed before held-out evaluation. Missing required coverage prevents a supported score; an unavailable optional factor will be omitted consistently within a comparison. Results will show contributing factors and uncertainty rather than claiming an optimal partner or guaranteed match wins.

## **ABET Complexity Factors**

### **Involving wide-ranging or conflicting technical issues.**

Our solution will balance multiple competing technical concerns. We need to balance the accuracy of our computer vision model with the quality of the user’s ~~Iphone~~ iPhone camera. We also need to make it easy for the user to set up their camera, while making sure the resulting analysis is still accurate. ~~Additionally, the more~~ Additional data ~~we collect, the more accurate our recommendations will be, however this will also increase the processing time~~ and ~~system complexity- the same goes for~~ more complex matching ~~algorithms.~~ algorithms may improve recommendations, but can also increase processing time, recording effort, and system complexity. We will test whether those changes improve held-out results.

### **Having no obvious solution.**

There is no standard formula for determining whether two pickleball players are complementary doubles partners. We will need to determine how movement, court coverage, shot strengths, handedness, and court-side preferences should contribute to a partner recommendation. The project will also require experimentation to determine how well these factors predict effective pairings compared with simpler approaches such as overall skill ratings.

### **Including many component parts or sub-problems.**

The system includes several connected technical components, including camera calibration, player and ball tracking, court-coordinate mapping, court coverage analysis, shot-strength analysis, player profile generation, ~~roster management,~~ candidate filtering, partner ranking, data persistence, access control, and explainable recommendations. These components must work together in a complete pipeline from recorded drill footage to a final partner recommendation.

### **Involving multiple disciplines.**

The project combines several technical and non-technical disciplines. Computer vision is required for analyzing recorded drills, geometry is needed for mapping video coordinates to the court, statistics and machine learning are used to measure player performance and compare pairings, and software/cloud engineering is needed to store and process the data. The project also depends on pickleball strategy and team management concepts so that the recommendations are meaningful to players and coaches.

## **System Requirements**

• **SR-1:** Player Profile Generation- The system will generate and store a player profile containing relevant player attributes and measured drill results, court coverage, shot-strength, handedness, preferred side, and other information used for partner evaluation.

• **SR-2:** Court Coverage Analysis- The system will use recorded drill data to estimate and visualize the areas of the court that a player can effectively cover under defined scenarios. Results will identify the tested scenarios, usable sample counts, and uncertainty.

• **SR-3:** Shot Strength Analysis- The system will calculate and store performance metrics for selected shot types or directions, including measurements such as forehand and backhand success rates.

• **SR-4:** Camera Calibration- The system will calibrate recorded video to a pickleball court coordinate system so that estimated player ground-contact positions and observed ball landing locations can be mapped from image coordinates to physical court positions. Airborne ball positions require separate analysis and will not be treated as points on the court plane \[12\].

• **SR-5:** ~~Roster and Team~~ Partner Candidate Selection- The system will allow ~~authorized collegiate team users~~ players to ~~maintain an eligible roster,~~ filter registered candidates by supported preferences and compare potential doubles ~~pairings, and use player-profile information to support team-selection decisions.~~ pairings using their assessment profiles.

• **SR-6:** Data Persistence- The system will persist player profiles, drill results, coverage measurements, ~~roster information,~~ matching preferences, and generated recommendations so that data remains available across application sessions.

• **SR-7:** Explainable recommendations- The system will generate partner recommendations based on complementary movement and shot strengths and provide explanations showing the measurements and coverage characteristics that contributed to each recommendation.

• **SR-8:** Data Access management- The system will restrict access to player profiles, recorded footage, team data, and recommendations based on authenticated user roles and permissions. Players will control whether their matching profile is discoverable; raw recordings will remain private.

• **SR-9:** Result Review- The system will let players inspect attempt evidence, flag questionable outcomes, and repeat affected drills before relying on those results for recommendations. Flagged attempts will retain their original predictions and exclusion reasons.

# **3\. Project Objective**

The objective of this project is to develop a camera-assisted pickleball application that allows collegiate pickleball players to select doubles partners with complementary movement and shot strengths. Each player will complete a set of recorded drills that will create player ~~profiles, court coverage,~~ profiles and ~~determine optimal~~ court-coverage measurements used to rank eligible partner ~~rankings based on an eligible roster.~~ candidates. Our solution ~~will be able~~ aims to ~~optimize~~ improve the ~~team~~ partner selection process, allowing players and collegiate teams to make data-driven decisions about pairings.

## **Data collection and evaluation**

We will recruit a pilot group of approximately 8–12 consenting players, subject to availability, and record the selected drills across repeated sessions. Team members will label player positions, visible ball locations, and attempt outcomes using CVAT. Two reviewers will resolve disagreements on the held-out outcome labels. Training, validation, and test footage will be separated by player and session so adjacent frames from one recording do not appear in different splits. We will benchmark pretrained models first and consider fine-tuning only if the results and available labeled footage justify it.

| Evaluation area | Proposed check |
| :---- | :---- |
| Court mapping | Measure player ground-position error against manually marked court locations; an initial target is a mean error of no more than 0.30 m. |
| Attempt scoring | Compare automatic outcomes with reviewed labels. An initial target is macro-F1 of at least 0.85 while retaining at least 80% of valid feeds; also report ball precision/recall and exclusion rates. |
| Repeatability | Compare the same player’s measurements across sessions and feed types; identify categories too unstable to support recommendations. |
| Matching usefulness | Compare coverage-based recommendations with a skill-only baseline using the same candidate pool and filters, controlled paired drills, and player feedback. |
| Usability and performance | Measure setup success, review effort, and end-to-end turnaround under documented phone, video-size, network, and server conditions. |

These targets are provisional and will be refined after the pilot, before the final test. Paired drills will be used for evaluation, while the application’s assessment workflow remains individual drills. We will compare successful returns, uncovered areas, and overlapping attempts across selected pairings, using comparable feeds and varied testing order. Player ratings of explanation clarity will supplement performance measurements. If the added coverage data does not improve on skill-only matching, we will report that result and revise the scoring model; a small pilot cannot establish improved tournament win rates.

# **5\. Competitive Analysis**

## **5.1 PB Vision**

**Overview:** PB Vision offers video-based pickleball analysis and coaching, keeping track of player and shot positioning for ~~singles and~~ doubles play to provide performance ratings and suggested areas for improvement. \[4\]

URL: https\://pb.vision/

### **SWOT Analysis**

**Strengths:** PB Vision offers an all-in-one approach to game analysis and coaching, ~~making users more likely~~ which may appeal to ~~use it exclusively rather than~~ players seeking performance feedback in ~~conjunction with competing products.~~ one service \[4\]. Additionally, it can use video recorded on a smartphone, reducing the need for expensive dedicated equipment.

**Weaknesses:** The product attempts to provide an objective rating of a player’s skill, ~~but~~ and its Ratings Report can compare tagged players. The reviewed documentation does not ~~feature tools to compare one’s performance against that of other players.~~ establish individual-drill-based partner recommendations, which is the specific use case our project will investigate \[4\].

**Opportunities:** Pickleball’s increasing popularity in general, along with its popularity among technology enthusiasts, ~~means that there is a market willing and eager~~ may expand its potential audience; willingness to ~~use an automated analysis and coaching system.~~ adopt these tools still requires customer research.

**Threats:** ~~PB Vision operates on~~ Competing analysis tools and users’ existing coaching or rating workflows may limit adoption. We have not established a ~~paid subscription model with more expensive plans than other pickleball-focused products. The higher cost of the product may lead some users to seek out more economical options.~~ comparative pricing advantage for our project.

### **Comparison to Our Project**

Our project aims to take an approach centered more on competitive team play ~~while offering similar~~ using shot ~~tracking~~ and ~~player rating features as PB Vision~~ movement measurements with less of an emphasis on coaching. Similarly, both rely on video to assess player performance. By analyzing footage of ~~drills and games,~~ individual drills, our system will identify a team’s players’ strengths and weaknesses to build profiles on their performance, enabling ~~automatic~~ data-driven doubles ~~pairing selections.~~ partner recommendations. PB Vision already includes partner coordination metrics; our distinction is the proposed link from standardized individual assessments to explainable partner matching \[4\].

## **5.2 DUPR**

**Overview:** DUPR provides a solution for competitive pickleball players to keep track of their performance against others using a unified, verified rating system. \[2\]

URL: https\://www\.dupr.com

### **SWOT Analysis**

**Strengths:** DUPR leverages a network of coaches and event organizers and a score-based rating algorithm to ~~give players accurate ratings.~~ estimate player skill \[2\]. Its integration with external AI-driven tools provides players with greater flexibility in getting a rating. \[8\]

**Weaknesses:** ~~The service has no user~~ An overall rating does not directly describe direction-specific drill coverage. DUPR does offer a paid DUPR+ membership, so absence of a payment model ~~and relies on external sponsorships to remain viable.~~ is not a supported weakness \[8\].

**Opportunities:** With the growing prevalence of competitive pickleball, players inevitably wish to seek out an accurate, verifiable, and uniform rating system, making the market for this product readily apparent. Additionally, by partnering with established brands and leagues, DUPR has rapidly gained popularity, and thus credibility, earning it widespread adoption among professionals and hobbyists alike.

**Threats:** ~~Many stakeholders entrenched in this system are players~~ Alternative ratings and ~~enthusiasts, which~~ analysis products may ~~lead to allegations of conflicts of interest~~ compete for adoption. For our project, a key risk is that ~~could impact credibility.~~ skill ratings alone may already meet players’ matching needs.

### **Comparison to Our Project**

Our project intends to utilize a comparative rating system, like what DUPR does, or perhaps even be integrated with DUPR ratings for players. However, our system will have a wider scope than pure ratings, as it will use data on player performance and skill to provide insight into which players may be complementary doubles partners. The MVP can accept user-entered ratings with a source and date; direct DUPR integration remains optional and depends on ~~a team would be~~ authorized access. Existing ratings can narrow candidate comparisons and provide the ~~best duos partners.~~ skill-only evaluation baseline.

## **5.3 Swish**

**Overview:** Swish offers a platform for pickleball players and club organizers to manage events, form teams, create tournaments and leagues, update ratings, and more, reducing stress and improving efficiency of play. \[5\], \[6\]

URL: https\://swishsportsapp.com

### **SWOT Analysis**

**Strengths:** Swish offers a range of services related to logistics and planning for pickleball games. With tiers ranging from free-to-use to subscription enterprise plans, Swish’s platform caters to everyone from the recreational player to the multi-court-facility manager. It also integrates with many widely-used court booking systems and the DUPR rating system, ensuring interoperability between facilities. \[5\]

**Weaknesses:** Swish ~~requires users to manually select into games, tournaments,~~ supports automated matchups and ~~leagues, and so~~ manual adjustments. Its reviewed documentation does not ~~automate~~ establish video-derived court coverage as the basis for partner ~~selection and matchmaking processes.~~ matching \[6\].

**Opportunities:** By integrating with existing court booking and rating systems, Swish makes a strong case for new users who already use existing planning services or are looking to adopt one.

**Threats:** Swish’s product is not necessarily unique, and potential users may view planning themselves as a better alternative to using a dedicated paid service.

### **Comparison to Our Project**

Swish is similar to our project in that it facilitates play across an organizational level, ~~but it does not feature~~ while our proposed distinction is the ~~same~~ use of measured drill performance ~~assessment and data processing capabilities that we envision.~~ to explain partner compatibility \[6\]. We aim to build a tool that helps teams analyze their players’ performance and find partners for optimal performance on-court.

# **6\. System Design**

## **6.1 System Design Overview**

Our system will use a client–server architecture consisting of an installed mobile application, an application backend, background video-analysis workers, and persistent storage. Players will complete individual pickleball drills, receive a personalized court-coverage profile, and discover potential doubles partners. Recommendations will consider complementary coverage alongside factors such as location, skill level, play style, court coverage, and more. The specific drills and matching criteria will be finalized through research and stakeholder feedback. Any registered player with sufficient assessment data may be a candidate, subject to discoverability settings and the requesting user’s filters. Matching does not require a coach, captain, or tournament roster.

The proposed technology stack includes React Native and TypeScript for the mobile application, Python and FastAPI for the backend, and PostgreSQL with PostGIS for player profiles, analysis results, and location-based searches. Videos and supporting analysis files will be stored in a private Amazon S3 bucket. Supabase Auth will provide account authentication. The matching engine will initially be a module within the backend.

Video analysis will run separately from user-facing requests using Celery workers and a Redis job queue. This allows processing capacity to grow independently of the application backend. Celery supports distributing queued tasks to worker processes across machines. \[9\]

The main data flow will be:

1\. Prepare: The player signs in, selects a drill, and positions their phone correctly ~~either with~~ using a tripod or ~~cameraman.~~ stable phone holder. Live camera checks block recording until the setup passes.

2\. Record and upload: The player completes the drill using a human feeder or ball machine. The app uploads the recording directly to private storage using a temporary signed URL. Failed uploads can be retried without creating duplicate sessions.

3\. Analyze: The backend queues the session. A worker processes the video to estimate player movement, identify ball events, and evaluate individual attempts. If the camera moves or relevant events cannot be observed confidently, affected attempts are marked uncertain rather than forced into a success or failure label.

4\. Store: The worker saves attempt outcomes, confidence values, coverage measurements, and references to supporting footage in PostgreSQL; recordings and evidence clips remain in the private S3 bucket.

5\. Review: The player can inspect results and supporting clips, flag questionable attempts, or repeat the affected drill. Flagged or uncertain attempts remain excluded from matching inputs until sufficient reliable data is available.

~~5\.~~ 6\. Recommendation: The app retrieves results and requests ranked partner recommendations from the backend.

Our goal is to display results approximately one minute after recording ends, including upload and processing. This target must be validated with the following constraints: recording lengths, network conditions, and available compute. Drill definitions and analysis results will be versioned, and repeated processing of the same session and analysis version will not duplicate scored attempts.

Recording limits and the supported phone configuration will be documented after pilot testing. Initial validation will focus on selected iPhones; Android support remains a later compatibility evaluation. A green setup indicator confirms the required checks passed, but does not guarantee that every shot outcome will be visible or measurable.

Raw video is useful for reviewing outcomes and debugging analysis, but does not need to be stored indefinitely after measurements are extracted. We will provide deletion controls and a documented short retention period, chosen with player feedback before pilot deployment. Matching profiles will be discoverable only through the configured permissions; footage will remain private. Separate consent will be requested for any research retention beyond the normal period.

## **6.4 Major Components / Features**

• Guided Mobile Capture: The application will provide drill instructions, camera placement guidance, and live setup validation. Checks will assess required court visibility, player visibility, stability, and image quality. A green indicator enables recording; a red indicator blocks recording and explains the correction needed. Drill definitions will support prescribed and unpredictable feed stages.

• Court and Player Tracking: We will evaluate MediaPipe Pose Landmarker, based on BlazePose, as the initial player-pose model. It provides body landmarks for movement analysis. OpenCV will support court calibration and mapping estimated ground-contact positions into court coordinates. This mapping will apply to the court plane; airborne ball positions require separate treatment. \[11\], \[12\]

• Ball Tracking and Automatic Attempt Scoring: A separate ball-detection and tracking pipeline will analyze incoming feeds, returns, net-crossing evidence, and landing locations. It will classify attempts as successful, unsuccessful, invalid feeds, or uncertain. Uncertain attempts will be excluded from both success counts and total scored attempts; confidently observed misses will count as failures. Ball-model selection and scoring accuracy will be evaluated using labeled drill footage.

• Player Profiles and Analysis Records: The database will connect each player to their drill sessions, individual attempts, and versioned coverage measurements. Profiles will summarize performance by direction, court region, and drill conditions. Results will include usable sample counts and excluded attempts, with insufficient evidence identified explicitly. Recorded measurements will remain separate from self-reported attributes such as skill level or preferred play style. The app will show evidence and exclusion reasons so players can flag analysis problems and repeat a drill without requiring a coach to review every session.

• Partner Matching and Visual Explanations: The matching module will retrieve eligible players and compare their coverage profiles under consistent drill conditions. An initial configurable scoring approach will consider complementary strengths and predicted coverage gaps, together with selected location, skill, and play-style factors. The application will show ranked recommendations, individual and combined coverage visualizations, and explanations of each suggested pairing. Matching weights and claims about partnership effectiveness will require evaluation with players.

## **Languages**

| Technology | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- |
| TypeScript | Develop the mobile application, including recording workflows, player profiles, coverage visualizations, and partner recommendations. |
| Python | Implement backend APIs, video analysis, movement measurements, and the partner-matching algorithm. |

| Technology | Purpose |

| React Native | Build an installed mobile application for iOS and Android using a shared codebase. Initial recording validation will focus on selected iPhones; Android compatibility will be evaluated later. |
| FastAPI | Build backend APIs for profiles, drill sessions, upload authorization, analysis status, and partner matching. |
| Celery | Run video-analysis jobs in background workers, with support for retries and distributing processing across workers. |

## **Libraries**

| Technology | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- |
| MediaPipe Pose Landmarker / BlazePose | identify body landmarks for player movement analysis. This is our initial pose-estimation candidate; ball tracking will use a separate pipeline. |
| OpenCV | Process video frames, identify court markings, and map estimated ground-contact positions onto a two-dimensional court. |
| React Native VisionCamera | Provide camera preview, recording, and frame access for live camera-setup checks and green/red feedback. |
| NumPy and SciPy | Calculate movement statistics, smooth measured trajectories, and support coverage estimation and matching calculations. |
| PyTorch | Experiment with ball-detection and tracking models, including training or fine-tuning if needed. The specific model remains a research decision. |
| SQLAlchemy | Connect the Python backend to PostgreSQL and manage database models, queries, and transactions. |
| React Native SVG | Display court diagrams, coverage regions, and visual comparisons between potential partners. |

## **Tools**

## **Cloud / Server Technologies**

| Technology | Purpose |
| :---- | :---- |
| PostgreSQL with PostGIS, hosted through Supabase | Store profiles, sessions, attempt outcomes, and versioned measurements. PostGIS will support geographic queries for nearby partner candidates. |
| Supabase Auth | Manage registration, sign-in, and authentication tokens. The backend will enforce access permissions for player data and recordings. |
| Amazon S3 | Store private recordings, supporting clips, and analysis files. Temporary signed URLs will allow authorized uploads and playback. |
| Redis | Serve as the message broker between the backend and Celery workers. Persistent session status and analysis results will remain in PostgreSQL. |
| Amazon EC2 | Host the backend and analysis workers. GPU-equipped instances will be evaluated if needed to meet the processing-time target. |
